title: Maximum element
statement: Given a nonempty array of numbers, return its largest value. The array may contain negative values or repeated values. Return the value itself, not its position; a one-element array returns that element.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Sort all values and read the final element: O(n log n).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Keep the largest value seen while scanning.

pitfalls: Initialize from the first value so all-negative arrays work.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    return max(input)

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Given a nonempty array of numbers, return its largest value.
constraints: 1 <= n <= 2000; values are signed 32-bit integers.
exampleExplanation: 7 exceeds 3, 1 and 2, so it is the maximum.

title: Second distinct largest
statement: Return the second distinct largest number, or null if it does not exist. Distinct means repeated copies count as one candidate. For example, [8,8,3] has second-largest value 3, while [8,8] has no second distinct value.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Sort unique values; take the penultimate value: O(n log n).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Maintain the largest and second distinct largest values.

pitfalls: Equal maximum values do not count as a second distinct maximum.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Return the second distinct largest number, or null if it does not exist. Return null when the requested result does not exist.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; distinctness is by numeric value, not index.
exampleExplanation: The distinct values are 2, 4 and 5; 4 is second largest.

title: Check nondecreasing order
statement: Return whether every number is at least its predecessor. Equal adjacent values are allowed. An empty array or a single element is nondecreasing because there is no out-of-order adjacent pair.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Compare the input with a sorted copy: O(n log n).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Test adjacent pairs and stop at the first descent.

pitfalls: Equality is permitted: nondecreasing does not mean strictly increasing.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    return all(input[i]>=input[i-1] for i in range(1,len(input)))

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON boolean. Return whether every number is at least its predecessor.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; equal adjacent values are allowed.
exampleExplanation: Every adjacent pair is ordered, including the equal pair 2,2.

title: Deduplicate a sorted array
statement: Return the distinct values of a sorted numeric array in order. Keep one copy of each distinct value and preserve ascending order. This exercise returns the shortened array, rather than an in-place length as some interview variants do.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Insert each item into a set and convert back: O(n) extra storage.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Emit an item only when it differs from the previous item.

pitfalls: Only adjacent duplicates can be skipped because the input is already sorted.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    return [x for i,x in enumerate(input) if i==0 or x!=input[i-1]]

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Return the distinct values of a sorted numeric array in order.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; input is sorted nondecreasing.
exampleExplanation: Keep one representative from the runs of 1, 2 and 3.

title: Rotate array right
statement: Given {nums,k}, rotate nums right by k positions; k is nonnegative. A right rotation moves the final element to the front. Treat k larger than the array length cyclically, and return an empty array unchanged.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Shift one position k times: O(nk).
approaches.space: O(n) working copy; O(1) per shift

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Reverse the full array, then reverse the first k and remaining n-k values. Each reversal changes order without changing membership; the three reversals place the final k values before the first n-k.

pitfalls: Reduce k modulo n, and handle an empty array before taking a remainder.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    a=input["nums"]
    if not a: return []
    k=input["k"]%len(a)
    return a[-k:]+a[:-k] if k else a[:]

inputFormat: JSON object with "nums": array of integers, "k": integer. Pass this entire object to solve(input).
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Given {nums,k}, rotate nums right by k positions; k is nonnegative.
exampleExplanation: The last two values 4,5 move before 1,2,3.

title: Move zeroes
statement: Return a copy with zeroes moved to the end and other values in original order. Preserve the relative order of all nonzero elements, including duplicates and negative numbers. The returned array must have the same length and values as the input.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Repeatedly remove a zero and append it: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Compact nonzero values with a write pointer, then fill the remainder with zero.

pitfalls: Preserve the relative order of nonzero values.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Return a copy with zeroes moved to the end and other values in original order.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; preserve the order of all nonzero values.
exampleExplanation: The nonzero sequence 1,3,12 stays in order, followed by two zeroes.

title: Missing number from zero to n
statement: Array contains distinct integers from 0 through n with one missing; return it. If the input length is n, exactly one number from the inclusive range [0,n] is absent. The missing number may be 0 or n; an empty input therefore returns 0.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Check whether each candidate occurs in the array: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: XOR all indices, values, and n so matching values cancel.

pitfalls: The range is 0 through n, including n; use only 32-bit-safe inputs with XOR.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    x=len(input)
    for i,v in enumerate(input): x^=i^v
    return x

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Array contains distinct integers from 0 through n with one missing; return it.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; n distinct values selected from 0..n.
exampleExplanation: The range 0,1,2,3 is missing 2.

title: Longest consecutive ones
statement: Given a binary array, return the longest contiguous run of ones. A run is a block of adjacent 1 values, interrupted by any 0. Return its length, and return 0 if the array is empty or contains no ones.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Enumerate each starting point and count its run: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Reset the current run on zero and update a running maximum.

pitfalls: Reset the current run at every zero, not just the first zero.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Given a binary array, return the longest contiguous run of ones.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; every value is 0 or 1.
exampleExplanation: The final three ones form the longest run.

title: Stock profit with one transaction
statement: Given daily prices, return maximum profit from one buy before one sell, or zero. You may complete at most one transaction, and the sale must occur after the purchase. Return 0 when no profitable transaction exists, including inputs with fewer than two prices.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Try every buy/sell pair: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Track the lowest earlier price and best profit.

pitfalls: Selling must occur after buying; a declining market returns zero.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Given daily prices, return maximum profit from one buy before one sell, or zero.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; prices are nonnegative integers <= 1000000.
exampleExplanation: Buy at 1 and later sell at 6 for profit 5.

title: Array leaders
statement: Return values strictly greater than every value to their right, in original order. The final value is always a leader. A value equal to a later value is not a leader under this strict definition. Return the leader values in their original left-to-right order, not in discovery order from a backward scan.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: For each position, scan its entire suffix to check strict superiority.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Scan from right, maintaining the greatest suffix value. A value is a leader exactly when it exceeds that invariant.

pitfalls: Equal suffix values disqualify an earlier value because comparison is strict.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Return values strictly greater than every value to their right, in original order. The final value is always a leader.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; values are signed 32-bit integers; strict comparison.
exampleExplanation: 17,5,2 each exceed every value to their right; their original order is retained.

title: Maximum subarray sum
statement: For a nonempty numeric array return the largest sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray. A subarray must consist of consecutive positions and must contain at least one element. For an all-negative array, choose the least-negative element instead of an empty subarray.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Enumerate all starts and ends while accumulating sums: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Kadane: at each index choose between extending the previous segment and starting fresh. A negative previous sum can only hurt every segment that extends it, so discarding it is safe.

pitfalls: An empty subarray is forbidden; returning zero fails all-negative inputs.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. For a nonempty numeric array return the largest sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray.
exampleExplanation: The segment 4,-1,2,1 sums to 6.

title: Next lexicographic permutation
statement: Return the next lexicographic permutation; wrap the largest permutation to ascending order. Lexicographic order compares the first position at which two permutations differ. Preserve the multiset of values, including duplicates, and return the entire resulting permutation.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Generate and sort every permutation: factorial complexity.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Find the rightmost ascent, swap its pivot with the smallest larger suffix value, and reverse the suffix. Changing the rightmost possible pivot preserves the longest prefix, and the ascending suffix is the smallest completion.

pitfalls: The suffix is nonincreasing; choose the rightmost larger successor before reversing it.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    a=input[:];i=len(a)-2
    while i>=0 and a[i]>=a[i+1]: i-=1
    if i>=0:
        j=len(a)-1
        while a[j]<=a[i]: j-=1
        a[i],a[j]=a[j],a[i]
    a[i+1:]=reversed(a[i+1:])
    return a

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Return the next lexicographic permutation; wrap the largest permutation to ascending order.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 1000; duplicates are allowed; wrap the last permutation to the first.
exampleExplanation: Swapping the last two values yields the smallest ordering greater than 1,2,3.

title: Product except self
statement: Return an array where position i is the product of every input value except i. Do not divide. Use the original input values for every output position. Zeroes require special care: with two or more zeroes, every output is zero. The product of no factors is 1.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Multiply all other elements independently for every position: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Store prefix products, then multiply each by a running suffix product. Every other position lies exactly once in either the prefix or suffix, including zero-valued factors.

pitfalls: Zeroes require no special cases with prefix/suffix products; division would fail.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    r=[1]*len(input);p=1
    for i,x in enumerate(input): r[i]=p;p*=x
    p=1
    for i in range(len(input)-1,-1,-1): r[i]*=p;p*=input[i]
    return r

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Return an array where position i is the product of every input value except i. Do not divide.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 1000; every prefix/suffix product and output fits a signed 53-bit safe integer.
exampleExplanation: The products excluding positions 0..3 are 24,12,8,6.

title: Selection sort
statement: Return an ascending sorted copy of integer values using selection sort. At each position, locate the smallest value in the remaining suffix and move it into place. Preserve every value and duplicate; an empty array remains empty.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Repeatedly extract the smallest value into a separate result, removing it from the remaining list.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: At position i, place the minimum of the unsorted suffix. The prefix is sorted and contains the i smallest values after every pass. This is a learning exercise; merge sort is asymptotically faster.
approaches.space: O(n) returned copy; O(1) sorting workspace

pitfalls: Selection sort is generally not stable; equal records may change relative order.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Return an ascending sorted copy of integer values using selection sort.
exampleExplanation: Each pass selects the smallest remaining value, producing 1,2,3,4.

title: Insertion sort
statement: Return an ascending sorted copy using insertion sort. Build a sorted prefix by inserting each new value into its correct position. Shift larger values right and preserve duplicates; an already sorted input should remain unchanged.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Enumerate permutations and select the first nondecreasing one.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Insert each next value into the sorted prefix by shifting larger values. The prefix invariant proves correctness; sorted input needs only one comparison per item.
approaches.space: O(n) returned copy; O(1) sorting workspace

pitfalls: Shift strictly greater values to preserve the original order among equal values.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    a=input[:]
    for i in range(1,len(a)):
        x=a[i];j=i-1
        while j>=0 and a[j]>x: a[j+1]=a[j];j-=1
        a[j+1]=x
    return a

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Return an ascending sorted copy using insertion sort.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 1000; integer values; duplicates allowed.
exampleExplanation: Inserting the second 1 before 2 and 3 gives 1,1,2,3.

title: Merge sort
statement: Sort integer values ascending with stable merge sort. Split the array recursively, sort each half, and merge the halves. Stable means equal elements retain their relative order; return the complete ascending array.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Use insertion sort, shifting larger prefix elements for each new value.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Divide into halves, recursively sort each, then merge by repeatedly taking the smaller head. Each level processes n values and there are log n levels.

pitfalls: Choose the left value on equality to make the sort stable.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    a=input[:]
    def rec(l,r):
        if r-l<2: return
        m=(l+r)//2;rec(l,m);rec(m,r);t=[];i=l;j=m
        while i<m and j<r:
            if a[i]<=a[j]: t.append(a[i]);i+=1
            else: t.append(a[j]);j+=1
        t.extend(a[i:m]);t.extend(a[j:r]);a[l:r]=t
    rec(0,len(a))
    return a

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Sort integer values ascending with stable merge sort.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; integer values; stable equal-value order.
exampleExplanation: Merging sorted halves yields -1,0,3,5.

title: Count inversions
statement: Count pairs i<j with nums[i]>nums[j]; do not count equal values. An inversion represents two positions whose values appear in the wrong ascending order. Pairs are counted by position, including overlapping pairs; a sorted array has zero inversions.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Compare every ordered pair of indices and count strict inversions.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: During merge, a smaller right-half value is smaller than every unmerged left-half value. Add that remaining count and recurse for within-half pairs.

pitfalls: Use a 64-bit counter; inversion count can reach n(n-1)/2.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Count pairs i<j with nums[i]>nums[j]; do not count equal values.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; values are signed 32-bit integers; answer fits a safe integer.
exampleExplanation: The first 5 contributes four inversions; 3 contributes two; 2 and 4 each contribute one.

title: Dutch national flag sorting
statement: Given only values 0,1,2, return them sorted in one pass using low, middle and high boundaries. Maintain separate regions for values already known to be 0, 1 and 2. Return the full sorted array without using a general-purpose sorting routine.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Apply a general comparison sort.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Maintain zeroes before low, ones from low to middle, unknown values through high, and twos after high. Each iteration shrinks the unknown region.
approaches.space: O(n) returned copy; O(1) sorting workspace

pitfalls: After swapping a two with high, inspect the incoming middle value before advancing.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    a=input[:];l=m=0;h=len(a)-1
    while m<=h:
        if a[m]==0: a[l],a[m]=a[m],a[l];l+=1;m+=1
        elif a[m]==2: a[m],a[h]=a[h],a[m];h-=1
        else: m+=1
    return a

inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Given only values 0,1,2, return them sorted in one pass using low, middle and high boundaries.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; every value is exactly 0, 1 or 2.
exampleExplanation: Two zeroes, two ones and two twos occupy their three consecutive regions.

title: Count important reverse pairs
statement: Count index pairs i<j for which nums[i]>2*nums[j]. Values are signed 32-bit integers. The comparison is strict, and negative values are allowed. Promote before doubling in fixed-width languages to avoid overflowing a 32-bit value; count pairs by their original indices.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Test the doubled-value inequality for every pair.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Sort each half recursively. For increasing left values, the right pointer satisfying the doubled inequality only moves forward; count before merging.

pitfalls: This differs from ordinary inversions; use 64-bit arithmetic when doubling signed 32-bit values.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Count index pairs i<j for which nums[i]>2*nums[j]. Values are signed 32-bit integers.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; signed 32-bit values; comparisons use twice the right value.
exampleExplanation: The valid index pairs are (1,4) and (3,4), since 3>2×1.

title: Two sum indices
statement: Given {nums,target}, return indices of the first pair discovered by a left-to-right scan, or null. Scan the right index from left to right. Return [left,right] for the first match; if several earlier positions hold the needed value, use the most recently seen one. A position cannot pair with itself.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Test every pair of indices: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Look up the complement in a map of previous values. Before index i, the map contains only earlier indices, so a found complement always uses two distinct positions.

pitfalls: Do not use the same array position twice; look up the complement before insertion.
inputFormat: JSON object with "nums": array of integers, "target": integer. Pass this entire object to solve(input).
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Given {nums,target}, return indices of the first pair discovered by a left-to-right scan, or null. Return null when the requested result does not exist.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; values and target lie in [-1000000,1000000]; return null if absent.
exampleExplanation: Indices 0 and 1 contain 2 and 7, whose sum is 9.

title: Contains duplicate
statement: Return whether an array contains a repeated value. Two equal values at different positions constitute a duplicate. Return a boolean, with false for an empty array or a single element.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Compare every pair: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Track previously seen values in a set.

pitfalls: Repeated equal values must be detected even when they are zero.

def solve(input):

title: Valid anagram
statement: Given {a,b} containing lowercase English letters, return whether they have identical character counts. Order does not matter, but the number of occurrences of every letter must match. Empty strings are anagrams of each other, and unequal-length strings cannot be anagrams.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Sort both strings and compare: O(n log n).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Increment counts for a and decrement for b.

pitfalls: Equal lengths alone do not establish an anagram.
inputFormat: JSON object with "a": string, "b": string. Pass this entire object to solve(input).
outputFormat: Return a JSON boolean. Given {a,b} containing lowercase English letters, return whether they have identical character counts.
constraints: 0 <= each string length <= 2000; characters are lowercase English letters.
exampleExplanation: Both strings contain the same counts of a,n,g,r,m.

title: Majority element
statement: Return the value appearing more than n/2 times; a majority is guaranteed and input is nonempty. The majority threshold is strictly more than half of all positions, not merely the most frequent value. Return that value; the stated guarantee means no absent-result marker is needed.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Count all values in a frequency map: O(n) storage.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Boyer–Moore cancels different values; a strict majority survives. Canceling two different values cannot remove a strict majority from the remaining multiset.

pitfalls: Boyer–Moore needs the guaranteed-majority promise; otherwise verify the candidate.
inputFormat: A JSON array of integers. Pass the complete value to solve(input), without a separate length prefix.
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Return the value appearing more than n/2 times; a majority is guaranteed and input is nonempty.
constraints: 1 <= n <= 2000; one value is guaranteed to occur strictly more than n/2 times.
exampleExplanation: 2 occurs four times in seven positions, exceeding half.

title: Isomorphic strings
statement: Given {a,b}, return whether a one-to-one character mapping transforms a into b. Each character of a must always map to the same character of b, and two different characters may not map to the same character. Mapping a character to itself is allowed.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Compare equality patterns for every index pair: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Maintain mappings in both directions to enforce a bijection.

pitfalls: A forward map alone allows many-to-one mappings; check both directions.
inputFormat: JSON object with "a": string, "b": string. Pass this entire object to solve(input).
outputFormat: Return a JSON boolean. Given {a,b}, return whether a one-to-one character mapping transforms a into b.
constraints: 0 <= each string length <= 2000; use ASCII characters and a one-to-one mapping.
exampleExplanation: Mapping e→a and g→d transforms egg into add consistently.

title: Range sum queries
statement: Given {nums,queries}, return inclusive range sums for each valid [left,right] query. For every query [left,right], include both endpoint positions in the sum. Return answers in query order; the array does not change between queries.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Sum every requested slice: O(nq).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Build prefix sums once; answer each range by subtraction.

pitfalls: Inclusive [l,r] means prefix[r+1]-prefix[l].
inputFormat: JSON object with "nums": array of integers, "queries": array of integer arrays. Pass this entire object to solve(input).
outputFormat: Return a JSON array of integers. Given {nums,queries}, return inclusive range sums for each valid [left,right] query.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2000; up to 2000 queries; every query satisfies 0 <= left <= right < n.
exampleExplanation: The inclusive sums for [0,2], [2,5] and [0,5] are 1,-1,-3.

title: Group anagrams
statement: Group lowercase strings by anagram. Preserve group discovery order and word order within groups. Each input word belongs to exactly one group. Two words are anagrams when each letter appears the same number of times; duplicate words remain as separate entries.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Compare each word with existing groups using repeated sorting.

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Use a 26-count signature as the map key.

pitfalls: Separate frequency counts with delimiters to prevent signature collisions.

title: Longest consecutive sequence
statement: Given an integer array, return the length of its longest sequence of consecutive integer values, regardless of input order. Return the length of the longest consecutive sequence, not the sequence itself. Duplicates do not extend a sequence, and consecutive values need not occupy adjacent input positions.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Sort distinct values and scan: O(n log n).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Start a walk only at values with no predecessor so each value is visited at most once. Every integer belongs to exactly one maximal run whose first value has no predecessor.

pitfalls: Begin a streak only when x-1 is absent; otherwise repeated walks become quadratic.

outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Return the longest set of consecutive integer values, regardless of input order.

title: Count subarrays summing to k
statement: Given {nums,k}, count contiguous nonempty subarrays with sum k. Count ranges of indices, so overlapping ranges and ranges with identical values are counted separately. Negative numbers and zeroes are allowed; the empty range is excluded.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Enumerate all subarrays: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: For each prefix sum, count earlier prefixes differing by k. A subarray sum equals the difference of its ending and preceding prefix sums.

pitfalls: Insert the empty prefix with count one to count ranges starting at index zero.
inputFormat: JSON object with "nums": array of integers, "k": integer. Pass this entire object to solve(input).
outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Given {nums,k}, count contiguous nonempty subarrays with sum k.
exampleExplanation: The two matching ranges are indices [0,1] and [1,2].

title: Longest zero-sum subarray
statement: Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray with sum zero. The result is a length, not a count of matching ranges. Negative numbers are allowed, and return 0 if no nonempty zero-sum range exists.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Accumulate every start/end pair: O(n²).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Store the earliest index of every prefix sum; equal prefixes enclose a zero-sum range. For a fixed ending index, the earliest equal prefix maximizes the enclosed length.

pitfalls: Keep the earliest prefix-sum index, not the most recent.

outputFormat: Return a JSON integer. Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray with sum zero.

title: Top k frequent values
statement: Given {nums,k}, return k most frequent values, frequency descending and value ascending on ties. Count each distinct integer once as a candidate, then order candidates by decreasing frequency and increasing numeric value when frequencies tie. Return exactly k values in that deterministic order.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: For each distinct value scan the full array to count it: O(nu).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: Count once, then sort unique keys by frequency and tie rule. A size-k heap improves selection when k is small.

def solve(input):
    import heapq
    h=[(row[0],i,0) for i,row in enumerate(input)]; heapq.heapify(h)
    high=max(row[0] for row in input); best=[h[0][0],high]
    while h:
        v,i,j=heapq.heappop(h)
        if (high-v,v)<(best[1]-best[0],best[0]):best=[v,high]
        if j+1==len(input[i]):break
        x=input[i][j+1]; high=max(high,x); heapq.heappush(h,(x,i,j+1))
    return best

def solve(input):
    n=input['n'];p=list(range(n));sz=[1]*n
    def find(x):
     while p[x]!=x:p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x]

    def union(a,b):

     if a==b:return False

title: KMP first substring match
statement: Given {text,pattern}, return the first matching start index, or -1. Empty pattern returns 0.

approaches.name: Baseline
approaches.steps: Compare pattern at each possible starting position: O(nm).

approaches.name: Preferred approach
approaches.steps: KMP prefix lengths let mismatches reuse the longest already-matched prefix instead of restarting. The prefix table preserves exactly the longest candidate prefix compatible with the suffix already read.

pitfalls: After mismatch, fall back through prefix lengths without moving the text index prematurely.

solutions.python:
def solve(input):
    s=input['text'];p=input['pattern']
    if not p:return 0
    lps=[0]*len(p);j=0
    for i in range(1,len(p)):
     while j and p[i]!=p[j]:j=lps[j-1]
     if p[i]==p[j]:j+=1
     lps[i]=j
    j=0
    for i,c in enumerate(s):
     while j and c!=p[j]:j=lps[j-1]
     if c==p[j]:j+=1
     if j==len(p):return i-j+1
    return -1
